title: Fiber vs. Wireless: Which Is Right for Your Network?
summary: Explore the evolving debate between fiber and fixed wireless technologies in network deployment, focusing on capacity, cost, and installation challenges.
body_markdown:
Fiber or wireless? If you’ve been around this industry awhile, you know that conventional wisdom was simple: “if you can build fiber, build fiber.” With today’s high-capacity wireless technologies, rising fiber construction costs, and growing pressure to get networks up and running faster, the answer isn’t so clear-cut anymore. Sometimes fiber wins. Sometimes wireless makes more sense. And sometimes, the smartest network uses both. So what really determines the right choice?


Fiber still offers tremendous capacity and long-term scalability, but we all know it comes with its own “baggage.” And today’s modern wireless is no longer just the option you turn to when fiber isn’t available. E-band, microwave, millimeter wave (mmWave), and multiband technologies can deliver multi-gigabit capacity and low latency, often with faster deployment and lower costs than building a new fiber route.


Just look at the numbers. The 2025


[Fiber Deployment Cost Annual Report](https://www.cartesian.com/fiber-deployment-cost-annual-report-2025/) found median U.S. fiber deployment costs of


**$18 per foot underground and $8 per foot aerial** . And 92% of respondents reported higher costs in 2025.


But those are only the starting numbers.


Every route brings its own challenges. Maybe there’s a river to cross. A mountain in the way. A highway, railway, or five miles of rural road. Or maybe it’s a busy city street where nobody wants another construction crew digging up the pavement.


Suddenly, this isn’t just a technology decision. It’s a route decision.


**So perhaps the better question isn’t “fiber or wireless?” but rather, what does this particular route require, and what’s the smartest way to deliver it?**


## The Short Answer


There isn’t one right answer for every route. And that’s exactly the point.


- **Choose fiber** for core, aggregation, data-center, and other very-high-capacity routes where fiber already exists or where the physical build makes sense.


- **Choose fixed wireless** when the route is difficult, the site is remote, or deployment time matters. Today’s E-band systems can deliver up to 10 Gbps with a single radio and up to 20 Gbps in a 2+0 XPIC configuration.


- **Choose both** when resilience matters. A separately engineered wireless link can provide a physically independent path that doesn’t share the fiber route’s conduit, pole line, bridge crossing, or other physical infrastructure.


## Fiber vs. Wireless at a Glance


Planning Factor Fiber Fixed Wireless


Capacity Extremely high capacity with substantial long-term scalability. Multi-gigabit capacity: up to 25 Gbps with a single E-band radio (Ceragon IP-100E) and up to 40 Gbps with two units in an XPIC configuration. Performance depends on spectrum, distance, and link design.


Deployment model Requires a continuous physical cable route. Requires suitable sites and an engineered radio path.


U.S. cost benchmark Median $18 per foot underground and $8 per foot aerial for labor and materials (FBA/Cartesian, 2025). Costs include radios, antennas, mounting, spectrum, power, installation, and engineering; costs do not scale per foot of route. Where new fiber construction is costly or complex, fixed wireless can offer substantial deployment savings and a faster path to revenue. Actual costs and payback depend on the route, equipment, and network requirements.


Deployment speed Affected by rights-of-way, permits, utility locates, and construction. Permitting timelines ran about 20% longer than in prior years. Can go live in days to weeks where sites, spectrum, and radio conditions are suitable.


Difficult terrain The physical route must cross or go around obstacles. Can cross many physical obstacles where a viable radio path exists.


Propagation delay About 4.9 µs per km; light in glass travels at roughly two-thirds the speed of light in a vacuum. About 3.3 µs per km on a direct path. End-to-end latency depends on network architecture.


Availability High when properly engineered, but exposed to physical route failures. Carrier-grade links can be designed for 99.999% availability, accounting for propagation and interference.


Resilience Requires genuinely diverse physical routes. Can provide an independent path around the fiber route.


Strong fit Existing fiber, core and aggregation networks, high-capacity routes, and long-term infrastructure. Difficult-to-fiber locations, rapid expansion, rural and remote sites, network extension, and path diversity.


## Installation Time: How Quickly Does the Network Need to Go Live?


If fiber already reaches the site, activation can be relatively straightforward.


Building a new route from scratch is a different story. Before traffic moves, there may be route engineering, rights-of-way, permits, utility locates, trenching or boring, pole make-ready, splicing, testing, and restoration. The 2025 FBA/Cartesian report found that permitting extended project timelines by about 20%, with some respondents reporting delays of up to 18 months. More than half of underground crews were also progressing at less than 1,000 feet per day.


Put that against a 5-mile route. At 1,000 feet per day, you’re already looking at roughly 26 crew days of construction before permitting, locates, restoration, and the other work surrounding the build.


Suddenly, “just build fiber” doesn’t sound quite so simple.


Wireless doesn’t eliminate engineering work. You still need suitable sites. You need spectrum. You need mounting, power, path engineering, alignment, and sufficient fade margin. With fiber, you have to build a continuous physical route between the endpoints. With wireless, you engineer a radio path between them.


For the right route, that can take a lot of time and construction out of the equation.


Wireless can also get traffic moving while a longer fiber project continues. And once fiber arrives, the radio link doesn’t necessarily have to come down. It can remain in place as a physically diverse path.


Long story short, getting fiber eventually doesn’t mean you have to wait for connectivity today.


## Fiber vs. Wireless Capacity: How Much Can Wireless Deliver?


There’s a reason fiber anchors so many core and aggregation networks: its capacity ceiling is extremely high. But if you still think “wireless” automatically means “lower capacity,” it may be time to update that picture.


- **E-band:** Channels up to 2 GHz wide support multi-gigabit transport. Ceragon’s


[IP-50E](https://www.ceragon.com/products/ip-50e) and


[IP-50EX Series](https://www.ceragon.com/products/ip-50ex?utm_source=chatgpt.com) provide high-capacity E-band connectivity, supporting up to


**10 Gbps with a single radio and up to 20 Gbps in a 2+0 XPIC configuration** , while the


[IP-100E](https://www.ceragon.com/products/ip-100e) extends E-band capacity to


**25 Gbps with a single radio and up to 40 Gbps with two units in XPIC** .


- **Multiband:** Pairing E-band with microwave extends reach without giving up availability. Ceragon’s layer 1aggregation enables multiband and even multivendor links.


- **In the field:**[Ayera Technologies (a California-based ISP)](https://www.ceragon.com/hubfs/Case%20Studies/02_CS_ISPs_Ayera%20WISP%20%281st%208020%29_NA_Final.pdf) doubled a two-mile backbone link from 10 to 20 Gbps with four Siklu by Ceragon EH-8020FX radios in 2+0 XPIC configuration, with no additional spectrum and no FCC update. That’s 20 Gbps across a route without laying a new fiber path.


- [Rural 5G (Tier-1 U.S. operator)](https://www.ceragon.com/resources/case-studies/tier1-carrier-delivers-max-capacity-with-mmw-link-auto-aligner) **:** Microwave plus E-band multiband delivered 10 Gbps backhaul with near-zero downtime and cost advantages over fiber.


- [ISP capacity (Fybercom)](https://www.ceragon.com/case-study/fybercom-ip-50exp-rural-broadband) **:** Ceragon’s IP-50EXP delivered typical throughput of


**9.1–9.9 Gbps over a 13.8-mile (22.2 km) rural link** , using a 3 ft. antenna alongside its existing 11 GHz microwave link.


- [Smart city (City of Mesa, Arizona)](https://www.ceragon.com/hubfs/Resource_Center_/Case_Studies_/14_CS_Smart%20City_City%20of%20Mesa_Signify_NA.pdf) **:** 400+ Siklu by Ceragon MultiHaul™ TG mmWave nodes across roughly six square miles, with full gigabit throughput across multiple hops.


- **Fiber vs. wireless**


**is a route-by-route decision.**


Fiber offers exceptional capacity and scalability, while fixed wireless can be the smarter choice when deployment time, terrain, cost, or physical path diversity changes the equation.


- **Construction**


**economics**


**matters** **.**


Median U.S. fiber deployment costs are $18/ft underground and $8/ft aerial, or approximately $475,000 and $211,000 for a 5-mile route, respectively, based on reported labor and materials costs.


- Modern wireless is a high-capacity, resilient option. E-band and multiband technologies deliver multi-gigabit connectivity and can provide a physically independent path alongside fiber.


- **The myth of fiber is not that fiber is bad. Fiber is essential. The myth is treating it as the only practical answer.**


So the question isn’t really whether wireless can “compete” with fiber.


**How much capacity does the link need?**


Once you know that, you can decide which architecture makes sense.


## Fiber vs. Wireless: What Does the Route Really Cost?


This is where the route really starts to matter.


The FBA/Cartesian 2025 report found median U.S. costs of


**$18 per foot underground and $8 per foot aerial** for labor and materials.


Put those numbers against a 5-mile route and they add up quickly.


Fiber Scenario (5 Miles = 26,400 ft) Cost per Foot Estimated Construction Cost


Aerial, median $8.00 $211,200


Aerial, typical range (interquartile) $4.90–$11.50 $129,360–$303,600


Underground, median $18.00 $475,200


Underground, typical range (interquartile) $11.50–$25.00 $303,600–$660,000


Underground, rocky terrain, median $22.00 $580,800


And, of course, five miles of easy terrain can be a very different project from five miles of difficult terrain.


The same report found a median of $22 per foot in rocky terrain and $20.38 in urban underground construction, compared with $11.88 in extremely rural areas. Permitting averaged about 10% of project cost, while aerial make-ready exceeded 150% of the construction budget in some projects.


That’s a pretty wide range. Why? Because you’re not just paying for fiber. You’re paying to create a physical path for it.


Wireless has costs too. Radios, antennas, spectrum, mounting, power, installation, and engineering all need to be accounted for. But another mile of radio path doesn’t automatically mean trenching, boring, or pole attachment.


For network planners, that changes the economics.


The harder and longer the physical route becomes, the more important it is to compare the cost of building the path, not just the cost of the transport equipment at either end.


## Latency: Look at the Complete Network Path


Both fiber and fixed wireless can support low-latency networks.


At the propagation level, light through fiber travels at roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, about 4.9 microseconds per kilometer. Radio waves through air travel at close to the speed of light, or roughly 3.3 microseconds per kilometer.


Across 50 kilometers, that’s roughly 245 microseconds of propagation delay through fiber versus about 167 microseconds across a direct radio path.


Does that mean wireless is always faster?


No.


Real networks don’t follow perfectly straight lines.


A fiber route may follow roads, ducts, bridges, or rights-of-way, making the cable path longer than the geographic distance between the endpoints. A wireless path may be more direct.


But switching, queuing, packet processing, protection architecture, and additional hops can add latency to either network. So “fiber is faster” and “wireless is faster” both miss the bigger point.


**Look at the complete path.** That’s the latency your application will actually experience.


## Ease of Installation: What Stands Between Point A and Point B?


On a network map, two locations can look easy to connect. Then you get into the field.


Maybe there’s a mountain between them. Or rocky ground. Wetlands. A river. A highway. Railway tracks. Private property. Multiple jurisdictions. Or a dense city street where excavation becomes a project all by itself.


That’s where route design gets interesting.


With fiber, those obstacles have to be crossed, avoided, bored under, attached over, or otherwise engineered into a continuous physical route.


With wireless, you’re solving for a different set of variables: line of sight, spectrum, distance, interference, mounting locations, antenna size, and availability objectives.


Neither is engineering-free. They’re simply different engineering problems.


For example, Ceragon worked with


[Fybercom](https://www.ceragon.com/case-study/fybercom-ip-50exp-rural-broadband) to deliver a high-capacity connection across a 13.8-mile (22.2 km) link. Using the IP-50EXP with a three-foot antenna alongside Fybercom’s existing 11 GHz microwave link, the deployment achieved typical throughput of 9.1–9.9 Gbps.


That’s nearly 10 Gbps across almost 14 miles of rural terrain, without having to build a new fiber route.


## Reliability: Redundant Doesn’t Always Mean Diverse


Let’s say you have two fiber connections into a critical site.


On the network diagram, that looks redundant. But where do those fibers actually go?


If they eventually enter the same conduit, travel along the same pole line, or cross the same bridge, one physical event can still affect both. That’s the difference between redundancy and genuine path diversity.


Fiber is highly reliable when properly engineered, but it still has a physical route. Excavation, construction, damaged poles, severe weather, theft, vandalism, and other events can interrupt that route. Ceragon’s


[analysis of the U.S. carriers’ STRIKE initiative](https://www.ceragon.com/blog/when-fiber-routes-fail-why-wireless-backhaul-belongs-in-your-5g-security-strategy) notes that network theft and vandalism incidents rose 59% year over year in 2025, affecting 11.8 million customers.


Wireless has its own engineering requirements. Path clearance, fade margin, antenna alignment, site stability, power, grounding, equipment hardening, interference, spectrum conditions, and weather modeling all matter.


But here’s the useful part:


**fiber and wireless don’t depend on the same physical path.**


A separately engineered wireless link doesn’t share the fiber’s conduit, pole line, or bridge crossing. For an uptime-critical site, that creates options.


Instead of asking whether you have two connections, ask whether you have


**two genuinely independent paths** .


That’s a much better measure of resilience.


## Security: Look Beyond Glass Versus Air


There’s a familiar assumption that fiber is inherently more secure because traffic stays inside a cable, while wireless traffic travels through the air.


But the medium is only one part of the security architecture.


Authentication, encryption, key management, access control, segmentation, monitoring, and operational practices matter in both fiber and wireless networks.


Wireless transport can encrypt traffic in transit and use secure management and authentication controls.


[Ceragon's IP-50EX](https://www.ceragon.com/products/ip-50ex) , for example, supports HTTPS, TLS, SSH, SNMPv3, advanced authentication, and optional AES radio encryption.


So the useful question isn’t whether the signal travels through glass or air.


It’s whether the complete architecture meets your security and compliance requirements.


## What About Aerial Fiber?


Not every fiber route has to go underground.


Where suitable poles already exist, aerial fiber can change the economics considerably.


The FBA/Cartesian report puts median aerial construction at $8 per foot compared with $18 per foot underground. Aerial crews also progressed at about 4,000 feet per day for six-person teams, compared with roughly 1,600 feet per day for larger underground crews.


That’s a meaningful difference. But aerial fiber comes with its own dependencies.


Operators still need pole access, available attachment space, make-ready work, and permits. And the new fiber may have to share that space with existing copper, coax, fiber, and other utility infrastructure.


Sometimes that works beautifully. Sometimes the make-ready work becomes the project.


So aerial fiber absolutely belongs in the comparison. Where suitable poles exist and the economics work, it can be a strong option. Where poles are unavailable, congested, or unsuitable, wireless provides another way to reach the site without creating a new continuous cable route.


## Fixed Wireless in Practice


Specifications tell you what a technology is capable of. Deployments tell you what happens when you put it to work.


From rural mobile backhaul to citywide connectivity, fixed wireless is already solving a wide range of network challenges.


## Fiber or Wireless? Start With the Network Requirement


If Your Situation Is… Lean Toward… Why


Existing fiber, or a core, aggregation, or data-center route Fiber Highest capacity ceiling and longest service life where the route already exists or is justified.


New route across rivers, mountains, highways, or dense city streets Wireless Avoids continuous construction, permitting, and restoration along the whole path.


Service must go live in weeks, not quarters Wireless (then fiber later, if planned) Wireless can carry traffic while a longer fiber project proceeds, then remain as a backup.


Long distance to a few remote sites Wireless, or aerial fiber if poles are available Per-foot construction cost can dominate; radio costs do not scale directly with route length.


Uptime-critical site with a single fiber route Both A wireless link adds a physically independent path.


## Key Takeaways


**Fiber where it fits. Wireless where it solves the harder route. And both where resilience demands more than one path.**


- **Fiber vs. wireless is a route-by-route decision.** Fiber offers exceptional capacity and scalability, while fixed wireless can be the smarter choice when deployment time, terrain, cost, or physical path diversity changes the equation.
- **Construction economics matters.** Median U.S. fiber deployment costs are $18/ft underground and $8/ft aerial, or approximately $475,000 and $211,000 for a 5-mile route, respectively, based on reported labor and materials costs.


---


## FAQs: Fiber vs. Wireless


**1. Is fixed wireless as fast as fiber?**
Fiber has the higher overall capacity ceiling, but modern fixed wireless can deliver multi-gigabit throughput. E-band systems can support up to 10 Gbps with a single radio and higher capacities with multiple radios in XPIC configurations.


**2. How much does fiber cost per mile?**
The 2025 FBA/Cartesian report found median U.S. deployment costs of $18 per foot underground and $8 per foot aerial for labor and materials. That works out to about $95,040 per mile underground and $42,240 per mile aerial. Terrain, density, permitting, and make-ready work can push actual costs higher.


**3. Is wireless faster to deploy than fiber?**
It can be, especially when the alternative requires building a new fiber route. Fiber construction can involve rights-of-way, permits, utility locates, trenching, boring, pole make-ready, splicing, and restoration. Wireless still requires engineering, suitable sites, spectrum, mounting, power, and alignment, but it doesn’t require continuous construction between the endpoints.


**4. Which has lower latency: fiber or wireless?**
Neither is universally lower. Radio waves travel through air at about 3.3 microseconds per kilometer, compared with roughly 4.9 microseconds per kilometer for light through fiber. But actual latency also depends on route length, switching, queuing, packet processing, network hops, and protection architecture. The complete end-to-end path is what matters.


**5. How reliable is fixed wireless compared with fiber?**
Both can provide high availability when properly engineered. What differs is how they fail. Fiber can be affected by cuts, damaged poles, construction, and other physical events. Wireless needs to account for path clearance, fade margin, interference, alignment, weather, and power. Those different failure modes also make wireless useful as a physically diverse backup to fiber.


**6. Is fixed wireless less secure than fiber?**
Not inherently. Security depends on the complete architecture, including authentication, encryption, key management, access control, segmentation, monitoring, and operational practices. Wireless links can encrypt traffic in transit and use secure management controls.


The right choice comes down to capacity, cost, deployment time, and resilience requirements. Start with those, and the technology decision becomes much clearer.
